Written by Iqbal and Rahul Badwelkar , it 's as much of a love story as Kill was . Like Nikhil Nagesh Bhat 's 2024 gore-fest , love is not the story here . It 's a mere catalyst that sets the ground running . <p> The difference between Neelesh ( Siddhant Chaturvedi ) and Vidhi ( Triptii Dimri ) is on the nose from the second we see them and they see each other . She 's a wealthy Brahmin enjoying festivities at her residential bungalow . He 's one of the Dalit dhol walas her family has hired to play in the background . They have no business meeting again but they do , education being the great equalizer that it usually is in the case of such ill-fitting matches . They are both enrolled at the same law college . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forward her family 's legacy . Meanwhile , he wants to study what Babasaheb did so he can fight for his and his brethren 's right to live just like him . <p> Despite the many cuts forced by the censor board after a long-drawn battle , an unending disclaimer at the beginning that 's read out loud lest you get offended , and the inescapable , inevitable Bollywoodization of a blistering tale of oppression and resistance , Dhadak 2 hits like a speeding train . Iqbal does n't wince a moment to expressly show the unpleasant , the ugly and everything in between that is lived by countless Indians across the country every single day . <p> Chaturvedi returns to impressive form as a sincere , disadvantaged young man who 's been raised to believe that he needs to keep his head down if he does n't want it cut off . In spite of the tone-deaf , distracting decision to tan his face so he looks the part , the actor nails Neelesh 's complex interiority , his simmering rage , reluctant physicality , and tumultuous narrative arc @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an outsider in Hindi cinema lends itself beautifully to create an underdog you want to see win . <p> He finds a worthy companion in Dimri , who by now can take a masterclass in how to portray both strength and fragility in the same moment . She plays out with great skill the central conflict of a woman who knows enough to see beyond but not enough to see around . Although Dhadak 2 is primarily Neelesh 's story , the way Gully Boy was Murad 's and Masaan Deepak 's , Vidhi is just as essential as Safeena and Devi were to their films . <p> Not just the lead pair , the supporting characters also leave an indelible imprint . Take Neelesh 's parents , for instance . His father ( a terrific Vipin Sharma ) is a transvestite stage dancer and his mother ( Anubha Fatehpuria ) a community leader . Then there 's Zakir Hussain as the law school dean Ansari , that rare Dalit who managed to climb out of the bottomless pit he was assigned to at birth . <p> There 's also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the loose whose only agenda in life is ethnic cleansing . Finally , there 's Priyank Tiwari , who plays Shekhar , a Dalit student activist at Neelesh and Vidhi 's law school , closely fashioned after Rohith Vemula , the late PhD scholar at University of Hyderabad who killed himself on campus in 2016 , sparking nation-wide outrage over caste oppression . <p> At 146 minutes , the film is bathed in blue , the color of the Ambedkarite movement . Right from Neelesh 's name to the walls of his basti , the stoles that hang around the necks of Shekhar and other campus comrades and the paint he uses to write verses of protest that finally colors Neelesh 's face and his soul irrevocably . <p> Picture this . There 's a wedding in Vidhi 's family . She is dancing . As Neelesh watches her , he imagines himself dancing with her . But even in his daydream , he appears in the same ordinary clothes he 's wearing at the moment , he dares not show the audacity to conjure up a look more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And it 's one of the milder scenes where it 's only hinted at ever so slightly . Good men , we call them . <p> However , Chaturvedi 's winsome performance aside , I wonder if I would live to see the day when Dalit parts go to actors from the community and not Savarna heroes . Or is that too much of an ask ? Baby steps , I get it .

@@127663011 <h> From Holy War to Human Rights : Deconstructing the " Jihad is Genocide " Narrative <h> Share : <p> The discourse surrounding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is a minefield of charged language , where narratives are weaponized to define victimhood and justify violence . Within this landscape , few arguments are as totalizing as the thesis that the conflict is , at its core , a manifestation of an inherently genocidal Islamic Jihad against Israel . This perspective , forcefully articulated in polemics like Daniel Greenfield 's provocative article , " The Jihad Against Israel is Genocide " ( Jihad Watch , July 29 , 2025 ) , posits that the attacks of October 7 , 2023 , were not a political event but a theological ritual , and that Israel 's subsequent military campaign is a righteous act of civilizational self-defence . Any attempt to scrutinize Israel 's actions or apply legal standards is dismissed as a " moral inversion " orchestrated by the enemy . <p> This paper will deconstruct this incendiary narrative , arguing that it is a polemical distortion that relies on a dangerous misapplication of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a strategic erasure of Palestinian national identity and Islamic history , and the deployment of classic Orientalist and propagandistic tropes . By subjecting the " Jihad is genocide " thesis to the rigorous standards of International Humanitarian Law ( IHL ) , the nuanced tenets of Islamic jurisprudence , the lived realities of both Christian and Muslim Palestinians , and the powerful analytical frameworks of intellectuals Edward Said and Noam Chomsky , its function as an ideological tool to obscure political reality becomes clear . The refutation of this narrative will be built on three core pillars : first , exposing the double fallacy of misreading both international law and Islamic theology ; second , demonstrating the dual erasure of Palestinian political identity and the complex , pluralistic history of Islamic civilization ; and third , anatomizing the polemic 's ideological function while articulating an affirmative , humanist alternative grounded in Islamic principles . Ultimately , a path toward a just resolution requires moving beyond the simplistic and inflammatory logic of a holy war and toward a complex understanding grounded in politics , human rights , and universal legal principles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The central pillar of the " Jihad is genocide " narrative is its weaponization of the gravest charge in international law and its malicious mistranslation of a core religious concept . To claim that an entire religious concept is synonymous with genocide and that one side 's actions are inherently genocidal while the others are immune from scrutiny is to abandon both law and theology for political rhetoric . A sober analysis reveals that the slogan " Jihad is genocide " is a profound category error , a double fallacy that crumbles when confronted with the specific definitions of both its terms . <p> First , the legal half of the fallacy lies in the misuse of " genocide . " The term is not a colloquialism for mass killing ; it is a specific crime with a demanding legal threshold defined by the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide . Article II of the convention defines it as acts like killing or causing serious harm committed with the " intent to destroy , in whole or in part , a national , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( United Nations , Convention ) . This specific intent , or dolus specialis , is the crucial element that distinguishes genocide from other atrocities like war crimes or crimes against humanity . Proving it requires clear evidence of a systematic plan or policy of extermination , not merely inferring it from hateful rhetoric or horrific acts alone . <p> The actions of Hamas and other militants on October 7th were undeniably horrific and constituted grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions . The deliberate murder , torture , and abduction of civilians are war crimes . The hateful and anti-Semitic rhetoric employed by some Hamas leaders and found in its founding charter , which they later changed , could certainly be presented as evidence of genocidal intent in a court of law . However , to definitively label the attacks as genocide requires a competent legal body , such as the International Criminal Court , to prove that the specific intent of the operation was the physical destruction of the Israeli people as a group , not the achievement of political-military goals , however abhorrent the means . The narrative @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ genocide bypasses this rigorous legal process . More egregiously , the claim that " Jihad is genocide " represents a fundamental category error , conflating a complex and multifaceted religious term with a narrow legal definition , thereby indicting an entire faith of 1.8 billion people . <p> Conversely , the narrative 's outright dismissal of any parallel accusation against Israel as a " moral inversion " ignores a serious and ongoing international legal process , a process rooted in overwhelming and widely documented evidence . For nearly two years , the Israeli military has been relentlessly obliterating everything in Gaza . That destruction has not been hidden ; indeed , it has been meticulously documented by its victims and even boastfully displayed by its perpetrators . The Palestinians who live in Gaza , the majority of whom are refugees forced to flee what became Israel in 1948 , have been documenting every moment of the carnage . And in fact , Israeli soldiers have gleefully shared photos and videos of themselves destroying everything they see . It is this reality that forms the basis of the charge of genocide @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protest to the world 's highest courts and human rights bodies . It has been clear since October 7 , 2023 that the current Israeli assault is the culmination of more than 140 years of colonization , dispossession , expulsion , and repeated massacres . This is genocide . And it is this context that informs the ongoing legal scrutiny . In January 2024 , the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) , the UN 's highest court , found it " plausible " that Israel 's acts in Gaza could violate the Genocide Convention . This finding was not based on " Jihadist propaganda " but on evidence presented by South Africa , which included the staggering scale of civilian death and destruction and , critically , a series of public statements by senior Israeli officials -- precisely the kind of evidence required to establish genocidal intent . The Israeli government has openly and repeatedly declared its intent to annihilate Palestinians . Declarations by Defence Minister Yoav Gallant about fighting " human animals " and instituting a " complete siege " were cited as potential evidence of an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This legal scrutiny has been echoed and amplified by a powerful public consensus among the major human rights organizations in the world . Critically , B'Tselem , the leading Israeli human rights organization , along with Physicians for Human Rights-Israel have joined the international consensus in recognizing Israel is committing genocide . All of that sits alongside the United Nations bodies and many scholars of international law , human rights , and genocide and Holocaust studies that have also recognized the genocide . This chorus of expert opinion reinforces what B'Tselem and Human Rights Watch have already designated : that Israel 's systemic rule over Palestinians constitutes a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Rome Statute ( B'Tselem ; Human Rights Watch ) . The International Criminal Court has charged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with war crimes , and the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) case against Israel is ongoing . While Israel maintains its right to self-defence , its actions are still bound by the core IHL principles of distinction , proportionality , and precaution . The catastrophic civilian death toll , the destruction of over 70% of Gaza 's housing , and the weaponization of starvation have led many legal scholars and UN experts to argue these principles have been violated on a massive scale . As Norman Finkelstein meticulously documents in Gaza : An Inquest into Its Martyrdom , the pattern of disproportionate force against Gaza 's besieged population long predates the events of 2023 ( Finkelstein ) . By invoking " genocide " as a shield for one side while using it as a sword against the other , the " holy war " narrative abandons the universalism that underpins the entire project of international law , reducing it to a tool of tribal warfare . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assertion that " Jihad is Arabic for genocide , " a linguistic and theological falsehood designed to cast a core religious concept as inherently criminal . The Arabic root j-h-d signifies " to strive , " " to struggle , " or " to exert a concerted effort . " Its application within Islamic theology is nuanced and multi-layered . The most exalted form , which Prophet Muhammad is reported to have called the " greater jihad " ( al-jihad al-akbar ) , is the internal , spiritual struggle against the lower self ( nafs ) . This is the continuous effort to purify one 's intentions , overcome ego and vice , and live a life aligned with divine principles of compassion and justice . This internal striving constitutes the primary and most pervasive understanding of jihad in the daily lives of Muslims and is central to Islamic spirituality ( Ramadan , Islam , the West and the Challenges of Modernity , p.75 ) . <p> The external , and at times armed , struggle is referred to as the " lesser jihad " ( al-jihad al-asghar ) . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ qital ( fighting or warfare ) , that the most egregious distortions occur . Far from being a mandate for indiscriminate slaughter , the lesser jihad is governed by a strict ethical and legal framework within Islamic jurisprudence ( fiqh ) . The foundational Quranic principle is that fighting is permissible only in self-defence against active aggression . The scripture commands believers to " Fight in the way of God those who fight you but do not transgress . Indeed , God does not like transgressors " ( Quran 2:190 ) . The prohibition against transgression ( la ta ? tadu ) is a critical ethical constraint that classical and modern jurists have interpreted as establishing a comprehensive set of rules of engagement . These rules explicitly forbid the targeting of non-combatants -- a category that includes women , children , the elderly , clergy , and anyone not directly participating in hostilities . They further prohibit the destruction of civilian property , agriculture , and places of worship ( Abou El Fadl , The Great Theft , p.221 ) . The scholar Ahmed Al-Dawoody 's comprehensive study on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of non-combatants are central , not peripheral , concerns ( Al-Dawoody , p.47 ) . This defensive posture is reinforced by a clear Quranic preference for peace : " And if they incline to peace , then incline to it also and rely upon God " ( Quran 8:61 ) . <p> The horrific actions of extremist groups such as ISIS or Al-Qaeda , or the war crimes committed by Hamas , must be understood not as the fulfilment of this tradition , but as its flagrant violation . The targeting of civilians and declarations of indiscriminate war stand in direct contradiction to the Quranic prohibition on transgression . Mainstream Islamic scholarship has overwhelmingly condemned such actions . For instance , the Fiqh Council of North America issued a fatwa that unequivocally condemned terrorism , stating that " Islam strictly condemns religious extremism and the use of violence against innocent lives " ( Islamic Society of North America , p.12 ) . To use the crimes of these deviant groups to define the essence of Islam is a methodological fallacy akin to defining Christianity by the actions of the Ku @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ therefore a profound double fallacy , a collapse of both legal and theological integrity . <p> The Erased Subject : Denying Palestinian and Islamic Complexity <p> The " Jihad is genocide " narrative can only function through a crucial act of erasure : the denial of a distinct and diverse Palestinian national identity and , by extension , the denial of a complex and pluralistic Islamic history . If Palestinians are merely a faceless horde of religious fanatics acting out a 1,400-year-old script , then their political grievances can be ignored . This dual erasure reframes a modern national struggle for land and self-determination as a timeless religious crusade , a caricature that requires ignoring the rich tapestry of Palestinian society and the nuanced realities of Islamic civilization . <p> The most glaring casualty of this erasure is the Palestinian Christian community . As one of the oldest Christian communities in the world , their existence is a profound inconvenience to a narrative that paints the conflict as a simple clash between Islam and Judaism . Palestinian Christian intellectuals and theologians like Mitri Raheb and Naim Ateek have long articulated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but in the language of liberation theology and universal human rights . The influential Kairos Palestine document , authored by a coalition of Christian leaders , frames their cause as a quest for justice and an end to occupation , explicitly rejecting religious extremism . These Christians suffer the same occupation , the same movement restrictions , and the same violence as their Muslim neighbours , a shared fate tragically highlighted by the Israeli bombing of the ancient Saint Porphyrius Greek Orthodox Church in Gaza , where hundreds of civilians were sheltering . <p> Furthermore , the portrayal of Palestinian Muslims as a monolithic bloc of " Jihadis " is a gross caricature . For most of its history , the Palestinian national movement was led by the secular-nationalist Fatah party within the Palestine Liberation Organization ( PLO ) . The very notion of an " imaginary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ legitimate claim to the land and to a history of their own . As Palestinian Intellectual Sari Nusseibeh articulates in his memoir Once Upon a Country , Palestinian identity was forged in a shared culture and a shared experience of dispossession -- the 1948 Nakba , which saw 750,000 people displaced -- and the subsequent struggle for recognition and return ( Nusseibeh ) . Historian Rashid Khalidi has meticulously traced the development of this modern national identity over a century of continuous struggle against colonial conditions ( Palestinian Identity , p.23 ) . While Islamist groups like Hamas have grown in power , their rise is a political phenomenon rooted in the failures of the peace process , the entrenchment of occupation , and the desperation engendered by the suffocating blockade of Gaza -- a political reality documented by scholars like Olivier Roy ( The Failure of Political Islam , p.45 ) . This is the language of political manoeuvring , not immutable theology . <p> This erasure of the specific Palestinian subject extends to a broader historical erasure of Islamic civilization itself . The polemical portrayal of " over a thousand years of Islamic invasions , mass slaughters , slavery and mass rape " as the defining character of Muslim societies is a monolithic reading of history that ignores the complex reality of governance and interfaith relations . The more historically significant question is not whether Muslim polities engaged in warfare -- as nearly all pre-modern empires did -- but how they governed the diverse populations that came under their rule . A key institution was the dhimmi system , which granted non-Muslim monotheists ( " People of the Book " ) the status of protected communities . In exchange for a poll tax ( jizya ) , which exempted them from military service , dhimmi communities were guaranteed security , freedom of religion , and legal autonomy . While hierarchical , this framework represented a form of institutionalized tolerance that , for much of history , was significantly more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Europe . The historian Mark R. Cohen , in Under Crescent and Cross , concludes that the status and security of Jews in the medieval Islamic world were generally far superior to that of their co-religionists in Europe , who faced recurrent pogroms , expulsions , and forced conversions ( Cohen , p.145 ) . <p> Historical examples of this pluralism abound . The period of Muslim rule in Spain , Al-Andalus , fostered a vibrant culture of coexistence , a flourishing of science and philosophy fuelled by the collaboration of Muslim , Jewish , and Christian scholars , as detailed by Maria Rosa Menocal in The Ornament of the World ( p.156 ) . Similarly , the Ottoman Empire 's Millet System granted its vast Orthodox Christian , Armenian , and Jewish populations significant legal and cultural autonomy for centuries ( Braude , p.89 ) . <p> The Ottoman welcome of Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 is a powerful testament to this historical capacity for providing refuge ( Lewis 74 ) . The Islamophobic narrative also misattributed modern political tragedies to an ancient Islamic imperative . As Mahmood Mamdani argues in Good Muslim , Bad Muslim , explaining modern political violence through a purely religious lens is an Orientalist trope that ignores the legacies of colonialism and the imposition of the nation-state model ( Mamdani , p.34 ) . By acknowledging the reality of the Palestinian people in their diversity and the complex , often pluralistic , history of Islamic civilization , the conflict 's true nature is revealed : it is not a holy war , but a deeply political and asymmetrical struggle over land , sovereignty , and rights . <p> Anatomy of a Polemic <p> The critical frameworks of Edward Said and Noam Chomsky act as powerful intellectual antibodies to the fever dream of the " Jihad is genocide " narrative , exposing it not as sincere analysis but as a functional piece of ideological work . Said argued that Western discourse has historically constructed a vision of the " Orient , " including the Muslim world , as a static , irrational , and inherently violent " Other , " against which the " rational " and " civilized " West defines itself ( Said , Orientalism , p.287 ) . This process of dehumanizing caricature has long served to justify colonial domination . Greenfield 's narrative fits this mould perfectly . His depiction of Islam as a " fundamentally genocidal " religion whose followers are driven by a " transcendent religious experience " of killing is a classic Orientalist trope . It strips a complex civilization of its political rationality and historical agency , reducing it to a singular , monstrous essence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this analysis directly to the conflict , arguing that the denial of Palestinian history and their portrayal as terrorists was a prerequisite for justifying their ongoing dispossession . The " Jihad is genocide " argument is the contemporary apex of this dehumanizing process . <p> While Edward Said exposes the cultural underpinnings , Noam Chomsky 's work reveals the political function . Chomsky 's analysis consistently focuses on the vast asymmetry of power between a nuclear-armed , US-backed Israeli state and a stateless , occupied Palestinian people . The " holy war " narrative erases this asymmetry , portraying the conflict as a battle of equals , or even one where the vastly more powerful state is the underdog . This honour is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ethnic affiliation , establishing a theological basis for universal human rights . This establishes a profound ethical framework that makes the preservation of life a paramount religious value ( Ramadan , In the Footsteps of the Prophet , p.145 ) . <p> Contrary to the narrative of enforced submission , the Quran provides a strong theological foundation for religious pluralism . The text posits that human diversity is a deliberate part of the divine plan : " To each community We have appointed a religious law and a way . So race to all that is good " ( Quran 5:48 ) . As scholar Abdulaziz Sachedina argues , this promotes mutual respect over domination ( The Islamic Roots of Democratic Pluralism , p.123 ) . This principle compels believers to oppose injustice wherever it is found . These principles animate a global movement of progressive Islamic thought , from Abdullahi Ahmed An-Na'im 's work on Islam and human rights ( Islam and Human Rights , p.67 ) to Amina Wadud 's " gender jihad " ( p.89 ) . So , to continue aid to Pakistan , the US Congress approved the Pressler Amendment . This required the US President to annually certify that Pakistan did not possess a nuclear device . US Presidents Reagan and Bush certified the same till the Soviets withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989 . <p> In October 1990 , President Bush declined to furnish the Pressler certification , and the US reimposed sanctions on Pakistan . @@127687374 <h> Muslim world has met crises with rhetoric <p> When it comes to dealing with two of the biggest current crises in the Muslim world -- the devastation of Gaza and the Taliban 's draconian rule in Afghanistan -- Arab and Muslim states have been staggeringly ineffective . Their chief body , the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation ( OIC ) , in particular , has been strong on rhetoric but very short on serious , tangible action . <p> AMIN SAIKAL New Delhi August 2 , 2025 7:14 am <p> OIC <p> When it comes to dealing with two of the biggest current crises in the Muslim world -- the devastation of Gaza and the Taliban 's draconian rule in Afghanistan -- Arab and Muslim states have been staggeringly ineffective . Their chief body , the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation ( OIC ) , in particular , has been strong on rhetoric but very short on serious , tangible action . The OIC , headquartered in Saudi Arabia , is composed of 57 predominantly Muslim states . It is supposed to act as a representative and consultative body and make @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ globally . <p> It calls itself the " collective voice of the Muslim world " . Yet the body has proved to be toothless in the face of Israel 's relentless assault on Gaza , triggered in response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 . The OIC has equally failed to act against the Taliban 's reign of terror in the name of Islam in ethnically diverse Afghanistan . Despite its projection of a united umma ( the global Islamic community , as defined in my co-authored book Islam Beyond Borders ) , the OIC has ignominiously been divided on Gaza and Afghanistan . True , it has condemned Israel 's Gaza operations . It 's also called for an immediate , unconditional ceasefire and the delivery of humanitarian aid to the starving population of the strip . It has also rejected any Israeli move to depopulate and annex the enclave , as well as the West Bank . These moves would render the twostate solution to the long-running Israeli -- Palestinian conflict essentially defunct . <p> Advertisement <p> Further , the OIC has welcomed the recent joint @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the United Kingdom , many European Union members and Japan ) calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza , as well as France 's decision to recognise the state of Palestine . The OIC is good at putting out statements . However , this approach has n't varied much from that of the wider global community . It is largely verbal , and void of any practical measures . Surely , Muslim states can and should be doing more . For example , the OIC has failed to persuade Israel 's neighbouring states -- Egypt and Jordan , in particular -- to open their border crossings to allow humanitarian aid to flow into Gaza , the West Bank or Israel , in defiance of Israeli leaders . Nor has it been able to compel Egypt , Jordan , the United Arab Emirates , Bahrain , Sudan and Morocco to suspend their relations with the Jewish state until it agrees to a two-state solution . <p> Advertisement <p> Further , the OIC has not adopted a call by Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and the United Nations special rapporteur on Palestinian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from the UN . Nor has it urged its oil-rich Arab members , in particular Saudi Arabia and the UAE , to harness their resources to prompt US President Donald Trump to halt the supply of arms to Israel and pressure Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end the war . In a similar vein , the OIC has failed to exert maximum pressure on the ultra-extremist and erstwhile terrorist Taliban government in Afghanistan . Since sweeping back into power in 2021 , the Taliban has ruled in a highly repressive , misogynist and draconian fashion in the name of Islam . <p> This is not practised anywhere else in the Muslim world . In December 2022 , OIC Secretary General Hissein Brahim Taha called for a global campaign to unite Islamic scholars and religious authorities against the Taliban 's decision to ban girls from education . But this was superseded a month later , when the OIC expressed concern over the Taliban 's " restrictions on women " , but asked the international community not to " interfere in Afghanistan 's internal affairs " . This was warmly welcomed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and therefore most Muslim countries -- have adopted no practical measures to penalise the Taliban for its behaviour . <p> It has not censured the Taliban nor imposed crippling sanctions on the group . And while no Muslim country has officially recognised the Taliban government ( only Russia has ) , most OIC members have nonetheless engaged with the Taliban at political , economic , financial and trade levels . There are many reasons for the OIC 's ineffectiveness . For one , the group is composed of a politically , socially , culturally and economically diverse assortment of members . But more importantly , it has not functioned as a " bridge builder " by developing a common strategy of purpose and action that can overcome the geopolitical and sectarian differences of its members . <p> In the current polarised international environment , the rivalry among its member states -- and with major global powers such as the United States and China -- has rendered the organisation a mere talking shop . This has allowed extremist governments in both Israel and Afghanistan to act with impunity . It is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ how it can more effectively unite the umma . This may also be an opportunity for its member states to develop an effective common strategy that could help the cause of peace and stability in the Muslim domain and its relations with the outside world . <p> ( The writer is Emeritus Professor of Middle Eastern and Central Asian Studies , Australian National University ; and Vice Chancellor 's Strategic Fellow , Victoria University . @@127687458 <p> Gaza faces a dual crisis : relentless conflict and environmental collapse . The destruction of water and sanitation infrastructure has led to a severe water crisis , with millions of cubic meters of raw sewage contaminating streets and coastal waters . <p> Gaza 's survival systems are collapsing under a dual assault : relentless bombardment and an accelerating environmental catastrophe . What began as war has triggered a cascading ecological disaster , poisoning water sources , eradicating farmland , and trapping civilians in a toxic landscape where thirst , disease , and hunger are weapons as deadly as bombs . <h> The water crisis : A looming mass casualty event <p> The most immediate threat is the near-total annihilation of Gaza 's water and sanitation infrastructure . By early 2025 , over 85 per cent of wells , desalination plants , and pumping stations were destroyed or disabled with all five sewage treatment plants collapsing by late 2024 , according to Palestine Central Bureau of Statistics , March 2025 . <p> The consequences are visceral and lethal : millions of cubic metres of raw sewage flood streets daily and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cholera risks according to Natasha Hall , Anita Kirschenbaum , and David Mitchell . Compounding this , Gaza 's sole aquifer was already 97 per cent undrinkable by late 2023 according to Fred Pearce , while blockade-induced fuel shortages silenced most remaining water sources . <p> Only 40 per cent of pre-war water production functions which has forced families to rely on polluted wells or exorbitantly priced tankers , according to Reuters . James Elder , a spokesperson of ( United Nations International Children 's Emergency Fund ) UNICEF warns that children " will begin to die of thirst " as water scarcity becomes a life-or-death crisis , according to Jason Burke and Malak A Tantesh . <h> Agriculture ashes , toxic legacies <p> Gaza 's ability to feed itself lies buried under rubble and salt . A May 2025 , Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations ( FAO/UN ) survey reveals a moonscape : under five per cent of cropland remains usable , over 80 per cent of farmland is bombed , salinised , or mined , and 77.8 per cent of fields are inaccessible . Critical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ per cent of agricultural wells -- are shattered . The Strip 's breadbasket is now dust , forcing thousands into total dependence on aid . <h> Conclusion : The soil beneath peace <p> Gaza 's poisoned wells and toxic rubble epitomise a horrifying truth : environmental collapse is now a core strategy and consequence of modern conflict . Without centering water security and ecological restoration in peace efforts , the region faces irreversible disaster . As the Middle East heats faster than the global average , Gaza 's fate -- whether a shared recovery or a toxic ghostland -- will echo far beyond its borders . A lasting ceasefire , advocates insist , must begin with joint solar panels on shattered rooftops and clean water flowing across trenches . Survival , and perhaps peace , depends on healing the land first . <p> Tavish Bhardwaj is a former intern at Down To Earth <p> Views expressed are the author 's own and do n't necessarily reflect those of Down To Earth

Thyroid hormones decline , causing lethargy ; reproductive hormones also dip , often halting menstrual cycles . <p> People instinctively reduce their physical activity , not just out of weakness but because their bodies are essentially telling them to conserve every bit of energy . <h> Phase five <p> Eventually , fat stores run out . This can take weeks or even months , depending on the person 's initial fat reserves . <p> At that point , the body begins to consume muscle protein -- including muscles essential for life , such as the heart . <p> " The body tries to preserve muscle as best it can because muscle is very metabolically demanding to build , " Stephenson tells NPR . <p> " But ultimately , though , it gives up and says , ' I 'm gon na die if I do n't get protein here . ' " <p> The immune system collapses , leaving the body vulnerable to infections it can no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cause dangerous irregular rhythms , which can trigger sudden cardiac arrest . <p> Adults with water access can survive up to two months without food . But ultimately , in this fifth stage , unless food is reintroduced carefully , starvation becomes fatal . <h> Why children are the most vulnerable <p> Children deteriorate much faster under starvation . @@127716091 <p> In what may be termed as the huge cost of the Israel-Gaza war are the deaths from starvation and malnutrition-related conditions . Aid deliveries have often fallen far below the daily minimum needed to sustain the population -- at times dipping to just 10-20 trucks a day , compared to the pre-war average of 500 . The result is a humanitarian system that delivers just enough to avoid total collapse , but not enough to prevent widespread hunger , disease , and death . <h> How do Gazans get aid ? Why many die even while getting food ? Why is there malnutrition despite aid ? <p> Most of the food supplies Israel has allowed into Gaza go to the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation , an American group backed by Israel . From there , they walk to al Joura -- a sandy pit where families wait , often for 12 -- 24 hours , to receive a drone or military " go " signal to move toward the aid point . Once the signal arrives ( supposedly indicating safe passage ) , they proceed roughly another 1 ? km through lines of Israeli military checkpoints , sniper positions , drones , and barriers to reach the guarded gate of the distribution center . Witnesses have reported fire near or into al Joura -- even before the signal is given -- endangering crowds gathered for hours hoping for sustenance . <p> After the signal , thousands of people who have waited for hours ( often overnight ) in al Joura or nearby dunes begin sprinting toward the distribution gate to ensure they get aid before the supplies run out , often causing stampede . To reach the gate , people must cross 500 -- 1,000 meters of exposed terrain . This area is often surveilled by Israeli drones , surrounded by sniper or observation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Despite the " go signal , " witnesses say that gunfire frequently breaks out , either to control the crowd or for unclear reasons . The divide is particularly stark and glaring in disaster zones such as Gaza , where children go hungry for days , many starving to death . Inequality reigned till reforms threw in some correction . In France , the aristocracy enjoyed tax-free lives of opulence , while peasants were laden with unjust levies . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ specific climate actions from countries . It assigned specific targets to rich and developed countries to reduce their emissions in particular time frames , called commitment periods . <p> * Developing countries did not have any such targets , and were encouraged to take " nationally appropriate " actions to help the fight against climate change . This was in keeping with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities ( CBDR-RC ) , one of the foundational tenets of international climate law . <p> * This principle , in effect , says while the whole world has a responsibility to take actions against climate change , the bulk of the responsibility lies with rich and developed countries . That is because these countries accounted for the overwhelming majority of the greenhouse gas ( GHG ) emissions in the last 150 years , which have caused climate change . <p> * The Kyoto Protocol 's first commitment period ran from 2008 to 2012 , and the second from 2012 to 2020 . As a result , the world 's largest emitter , both in current terms at that time and historically , did not have any obligation to reduce its emissions . Several other countries , such as Canada and Japan , either walked out of the Kyoto Protocol at a later stage , or refused to accept binding targets for the second commitment period . <p> Previous year UPSC Mains Question Covering similar theme : ? ? The Khmer people were the direct ancestors of modern Cambodians , who still refer to themselves as Khmers . Their Kings constructed the magnificent complex at Angkor and governed much of mainland Southeast Asia , including most of modern-day Thailand ( then called Siam ) . <p> Preah Vihear bears the influence of Hinduism , the predominant religion of Khmer monarchs at that time . It also reflects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ surrounding region . Despite its Khmer origins , Preah Vihear has not always been under Cambodian control . The area it occupies has sometimes been governed or occupied by Siamese kingdoms and the modern Thai state that succeeded them . <p> In 1431 , as the Khmer Empire began its long decline , forces from neighboring Siam sacked the Cambodian capital at Angkor Thom . That defeat forced the Khmer King to consolidate his power closer to Phnom Penh . Over the next four centuries , Siam gradually chipped away at Cambodian territory , and by 1794 , a greatly weakened Khmer Monarch ceded control to Siam over the northwestern provinces around modern-day Sisophon and Batdambang . <p> STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD <p> Eventually , Cambodian King Norodom requested French protectorate status in 1863 , largely to avoid Siamese domination . Four years later , the King of Siam renounced his claim of suzerainty over Cambodia in exchange for large territorial concessions in northern and western parts of the Khmer kingdom , including the area around Preah Vihear . <p> The brief 1893 Franco-Siamese War saw Laos under French @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advances . In 1904 , the two signed a border treaty agreeing that the northern frontier near Preah Vihear would run along the watershed line of the Dangrek Mountains . That principle would have put most of the temple on Siamese soil , but the treaty did not state that . Instead , it provided that the precise demarcation would be agreed by a mixed commission . <p> In 1907 , French officials conducted a survey and produced a topographical map showing a border that deviated from the watershed line and put all of Preah Vihear on Cambodia 's side . The Siamese members of the mixed commission did not approve the French map , but neither did they conduct a competing survey nor raise a clear objection . <p> STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD <p> In 1941 , Thailand seized Preah Vihear and other areas as part of a wartime alliance with Japan . After returning the territory to France , Preah Vihear again changed hands after the defeat of French colonial forces in 1953 . A year later , Thai troops moved into Preah Vihear to replace the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) five years later which in 1962 issued a judgement in favour of Cambodia . <p> When Cambodian Prince Sihanouk in 1963 took possession of the temple , he emphasised the significance of the site to Buddhists in both countries and stated that Thais would be free to visit the temple without a visa , and permitted Thailand to keep relics taken from the site during the period of Thai occupation , even though the ICJ had ruled that the items should be returned . <p> However , in 2008 the historical dispute resurfaced when Cambodia sought to register Preah Vihear as a Unesco World Heritage Site . The SC , after all , is the custodian of the constitutional letter and spirit . As such , it is the bulwark against any encroachment of fundamental rights , including and especially free expression . In fact , the Court only has to look back on its own record to see why its current stance touches off concerns . It has established a rich tradition of checking executive overreach and protecting and upholding civil liberties . In earlier judgments , it has underlined , for instance , that " national security " can not be invoked as a ground to curb fundamental rights . In the 2021 case involving the alleged use of Pegasus malware against citizens , the SC held that while there are limits to judicial review when it comes to national security , " this does not mean that the state @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ national security ' is raised " . It accommodates and enables plurality , while enforcing rights and accountability . By laying down a singular definition of Indianness , by turning a restrictive eye on questions asked of the dominant narrative and the government , the Court goes against its own past record and does a disservice to the Constitution . That the oral observations of the Court are not legally binding , that they are only part of the deliberative process , is not a mitigating factor . The Court must recognise that it is a measure of the enormous respect for the institution of the judiciary that what it says is taken seriously -- and that , by the same token , in an argumentative democracy , it can have an undesirable chilling effect .

@@127888688 <p> Across time and cultures , the adage ' silence is golden ' has come to embody the virtue of restraint in speech . It perhaps originated in the ninth-century Arabic saying : " If speech is silver , then silence is gold . " The sentiment it conveys echoes in religious traditions , too . <p> Prophet Muhammad , as reported in Sahih al-Bukhari , advised Muslims to either speak good or remain silent . The Epistle of James in the New Testament urged Christians to be " quick to listen and slow to speak " . And in its 17th chapter , the Bhagavad Gita describes silence ( maunam ) as an " austerity of the mind " ( tapo maanasam ) . <p> Such pronouncements have strengthened the belief that silence is not the absence of speech , but the presence of meaning -- deep , intentional , and spiritual . However , this perception often overlooks the fact that what the aphorisms endorsed was judicious restraint , not muteness born of indecision or avoidance . In other words , silence is noble only when it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ great responsibility . When it accompanies oppression , it joins in the crime and becomes its voice . <p> Hence , Prophet Muhammad declared that the highest form of jihad is " a word of justice " ( kalimatu adl ) spoken against a tyrannical ruler ( sultaanin jaa'ir ) . Jesus too inspired courage in his followers saying : " What I tell you in the dark , speak in the daylight ; what is whispered in your ear , proclaim from the rooftops . " And in the Bhagavad Gita , Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that there is nothing more honourable than fighting a righteous war ( dharmyam sangramam ) to uphold justice . <p> Indeed , no serious philosophy upholds silence as a virtue when injustice demands a response . Yet , betraying its original nuance , the phrase " silence is golden " has been used to shield selfishness or cowardice , thus transforming silence into quiet hypocrisy . <p> Nowhere is this more apparent than in the political quiescence surrounding Israel 's ongoing assault on Gaza -- an onslaught that many experts now describe as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ razed entire neighbourhoods , and now threatens to starve a million innocent people to death , including countless children . <p> Silence in the face of these atrocities can perhaps be excused in lands where denouncing Israel brings the threat of imprisonment or worse . But what explains the silence of those who , free to speak , choose not to ? <p> Evolutionary psychology suggests that an intense fear of outsiders that prevailed among early humans persists even today because natural selection honed our protective instincts . In contrast , modern humans possess the cognitive sophistication necessary for negotiation or conflict resolution . Yet , they exhibit atavistic tendencies as if evolution had passed them by . <p> Scientifically speaking , behavioural modernity equipped Homo sapiens with remarkable cognitive powers such as abstract thought , complex language , social cooperation , cultural imagination , and technological innovation . These advances should have made us more empathetic and peaceable . Yet the paradox of our species is that we used the very intellect evolution granted us to refine violence . We expanded organised warfare , perfected weapons of mass destruction @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Among the non-violent majority , human fellowship failed in subtler ways -- through social identitarianism , propaganda , and ignorance of history . If most people today confine their solidarity to those who share their nationality , religion , or class , it is because disinformation-driven mistrust paints the ' other ' as a threat . As a result , even after being endowed with the capacity for unity , we chose division . <p> This moral failure often takes the form of silence , cloaked in specious justifications : that the victims are in a distant land ; that speaking out brings us no gain , while staying quiet costs us nothing ; that condemning genocide might endanger our interests ; that a single voice can not sway the oppressors ; and that our solidarity will do little to alter the victims ' fate . <p> But these are lame excuses . They are shamelessly invoked to avoid confessing the uncomfortable truth : we are silent because we do n't care . <p> Needless to say , it can not be denied that silence can , at times @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ holds only for the oppressed who are stunned into wordlessness by trauma . For those who watch from safety , silence is no act of dignity or courage . It is an abdication of social responsibility by which they not just surrender their freedom of speech but lose their humanity . <p> This makes reclaiming our humanity the biggest requirement for most of us today . But it is not an easy task . Mirza Ghalib had warned : " Bas ke dushwaar hai har kaam ka aasaan hona / Aadmi ko bhi muyassar nahin insaan hona " ( Because it is difficult for every task to be easy / Even man finds it hard to become human ) . <p> Indeed , to look human is easy ; to be one is not . Humanity is about preserving the humanitarian traits that nature has given us . The highest among them in the present state of affairs is our courage to speak for the victims of genocidal violence . We may find temporary refuge in silence . But in the end , silence is a verdict . It does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Faizur Rahman Secretary-General , Islamic Forum for the Promotion of Moderate Thought

@@127923119 <h> Share : <p> If you ever want to know what two countries really care about , do n't listen to the speeches . Watch what words they never quite say alone . In the case of Iran and Pakistan , one word keeps showing up as part of a suspiciously inseparable duo : " trade and security . " And when " security " is always lurking right behind " trade , " it 's a fair bet that commerce is not the real driver . <p> On paper , the relationship between Tehran and Islamabad should be one of the Muslim world 's great alliances . Two large Muslim nations , sharing a border of nearly 900 kilometers , facing similar economic challenges , and possessing overlapping cultural and religious ties . In reality , their history has been a masterclass in polite distance , occasional suspicion , and the kind of neighborly " cooperation " that tends to happen only when there 's a common problem to solve -- or a common threat to avoid . <p> Yet , in recent months , observers have noticed something @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , led by Chief of Army Staff ( COAS ) Gen. Asim Munir , has been exchanging warm smiles with the Islamic Republic of Iran . In February , Iran voiced strong solidarity with Pakistan during its border tensions with India . In April , Pakistan loudly condemned Israel 's 12-day military assault on Iran . To the casual observer , this might look like a long-overdue brotherly embrace . <p> It is not . <p> A Relationship Built on Sand <p> To understand why , we have to go back to 1979 -- the year that changed the Middle East and South Asia in ways still playing out today . Iran 's Islamic Revolution toppled the Shah , infuriated Washington , and created a Shia theocracy with a revolutionary ideology . Almost immediately , Saudi Arabia -- America 's indispensable ally in the Gulf and the self-appointed defender of Sunni Islam -- began countering Iran 's influence by funding Sunni religious movements across the Muslim world . <p> Pakistan , for its part , became one of the key battlegrounds in this Saudi-Iranian rivalry . While Islamabad officially maintained @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the ground was more complicated -- and bloodier . <p> By the early 1990s , Pakistan was suffering from a surge in sectarian violence . Extremist Sunni groups , many with Saudi funding , targeted Shia communities . Iran , in turn , was accused of backing Shia militant groups in Pakistan . The " brotherhood " narrative looked increasingly like a polite fiction masking a dangerous proxy war being fought on Pakistani soil . <p> The result was thousands of lives lost , an erosion of social trust , and a hardening of sectarian divides that still fester today . Whatever " warm " relations existed between Islamabad and Tehran were almost always transactional -- tied to moments when the two countries needed each other for security reasons , not because of some shared vision of Muslim unity . <p> The Imran Khan Interlude <p> When Imran Khan became prime minister in 2018 , he made no secret of his desire to uphold the nation 's sovereignty , to advance social justice , the rule of law , and human rights , and to have Pakistan be a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a crucial partner in that vision , particularly in breaking free from what he viewed as the stifling dominance of Washington and the Gulf monarchies over Pakistan 's foreign policy . <p> But Khan 's tenure coincided with intense regional turbulence : the US withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018 , the assassination of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani by an American drone in January 2020 , and escalating US -- Iran tensions in the Persian Gulf . While Khan managed to improve atmospherics with Tehran , his broader regional vision was cut short by his ouster in April 2022 -- a move widely seen as a Washington-backed regime change operation orchestrated by Pakistan 's powerful military establishment , which had grown uncomfortable with his independent streak . <p> The smiles , the handshakes , the press conferences about " enhancing bilateral trade " -- all make for pleasant optics . But the real conversation is about security , and both sides know it . <p> Iran 's position is straightforward , and it has been repeated in various forms for decades : stay out of our fights with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ activity off your soil , and do n't let your territory be used for subversive operations against us . <p> This is not an abstract concern . Tehran remembers very clearly how Washington , particularly in the 2000s , used Pakistan 's Balochistan province as a launchpad for anti-Iranian operations . These included support for Iranian Baloch separatists , covert backing of the Mojahedin-e Khalq ( MEK ) , and other militant outfits eager to cause trouble inside Iran . <p> The irony , of course , is that some of these same networks later turned their sights on Pakistan itself . After 9/11 , as the US military footprint in Afghanistan expanded , Baloch separatists and other armed groups became useful tools not just for pressuring Iran , but also for destabilizing Pakistan when Washington wanted to exert leverage . <p> Iran has long been aware of the double game . And while Tehran is pragmatic enough to maintain relations with Islamabad even under pro-US leadership , it also has red lines . As one senior Iranian official reportedly told Pakistani counterparts during the recent delegation visit : <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But if Pakistan restarts cooperation with the US in subversive activities from Balochistan , Iran will make Balochistan a nightmare for Pakistan . " <p> Balochistan : The Powder Keg No One Can Ignore <p> Balochistan , which makes up almost half of Pakistan 's landmass but has less than 6% of its population , is a perpetual headache for Islamabad . The province is resource-rich -- with vast reserves of natural gas , minerals , and a strategic coastline -- yet remains the country 's most underdeveloped and politically alienated region . <p> Contrary to popular perception , the majority of Balochistan 's population is actually Pashtun , not Baloch . One imagines the Pakistani taxpayer might be slightly irritated when her hard-earned rupees are being spent to monitor comments and ' likes ' on Facebook and TikTok . <p> Why Now ? <p> The sudden uptick in Iran -- Pakistan engagement is not happening in a vacuum . The Middle East is on edge . The Gaza genocide has dragged on , Iran and Israel are trading increasingly direct blows , and the US has repositioned forces across the Gulf . Gen. Iran knows Pakistan 's military has deep ties to Washington and Riyadh . Pakistan knows Iran has cultivated networks inside its borders that could cause @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " enhancing bilateral trade " because it 's the safe script . But beneath the surface , Iran is buying insurance , and Pakistan is trying to avoid opening yet another front in its already sprawling security crisis . <p> The truth is that in the geopolitics of this region , " brotherhood " is often a mirage shimmering above the desert . Up close , it 's just the harsh terrain of mutual suspicion , historical grievance , and pragmatic calculation . <p> The Pakistani military regime might think it can balance Washington 's expectations with Tehran 's warnings . But , what if all do n't give it much importance ? What if they choose not to pay the attention to higher tariffs on certain goods , Trump has threatened to impose , which are imported from them ? This increases total duties of Indian goods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ increase in tariff of whatever is imported to US also increases prices of the same for American investors , market , consumers and for whoever the goods bear importance within US . Slowly but definitely , it 's inflationary impact is likely to become more prominent in United States . Irrespective of whatever be logic deciding Trump 's tariff , he is apparently being over-confident by assuming that only his voice will echo , heard and then accepted by targeted countries . Regarding Ukraine-crisis , if President Trump is so concerned about continuity of a conflict , why has he chosen not to taken a similar stand on Gaza-genocide , prospects of which being heeded are stronger ? @@127956862 <h> Re-reading Waiting for Godot : Beckett , Darwish , and the Politics of Waiting in Palestine <h> Share : <p> Samuel Beckett 's Waiting for Godot is not merely a drama but a psychological , philosophical , and political reflection of today 's world . Published in 1952 , the play profoundly explores the notion of existential absurdism -- a philosophical perspective most notably developed by Albert Camus -- which confronts the tension between humanity 's deep desire for meaning and the chaotic nature of a universe that offers no such guarantees . In his seminal essay The Myth of Sisyphus ( 1942 ) , Camus -- one of the pioneers of existentialism -- defines " the absurd " as " born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world " ( Camus , 1942 , p. 28 ) . <p> In this two-act play , two characters , Estragon and Vladimir , wait for Godot -- a metaphor for divine salvation , meaning , purpose , or fulfillment -- who never arrives . This loss of sight strips him of his performative grandeur and practical dominance . He can no longer direct Lucky with precision or navigate the world without help . This reflects the inevitability of decline and the absurdity of hierarchical order in the face of time . @@127960701 <h> Israel 's many military conflicts reveal a startling trend , that global high-finance is turning wars into investments . @@127975278 <h> The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor is an ambitious idea that can cut shipping time by about 40% . But Israel 's war in Gaza poses a fundamental challenge <p> The IMEC being unveiled at the G20 Summit in New Delhi , 2023 . ( PTI/file photo ) <p> Earlier this week , India 's National Security Council Secretariat hosted envoys and officials from the United States , UAE , Saudi Arabia , France , Italy , Germany , Israel , Jordan and the European Union , to discuss progress on the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor ( IMEC ) . <p> The IMEC was announced during the G20 Summit held in New Delhi in 2023 " to stimulate economic development through enhanced connectivity and economic integration between Asia , the Arabian Gulf , and Europe . " <p> Its eastern leg will carry container traffic from India 's western ports to the UAE , from where high speed freight railway will carry goods across the Arabian peninsula ( UAE , Saudi Arabia , Jordan ) uptil the port of Haifa in Israel . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to ports in Greece and Italy , from where Europe 's well-established train networks will take goods to their final destinations across the continent . <p> What are the corridor 's ambitions ? What are some key challenges it faces ? And what is its future ? <p> Sound idea born in rare geopolitical window <p> In September 2023 , during India 's G20 Presidency , the IMEC 's conceptualisation and agreement was a testament to a remarkable period of stability in the Middle East . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Years of conflict along ideological and geopolitical lines ( Qatar-GCC , Iran-Saudi Arabia , Arab states-Israel ) had given way to normalisation agreements and rapprochements that prioritised regional economic growth . The Arab normalisation with Israel , which Saudi Arabia was set to join , was yielding enough geo-economic gains for Arab states to overlook the Palestine question and perhaps even explore minilateral arrangements with Israel ( on the lines of the I2U2 with India ) . <p> This rare geopolitical window allowed India and its Middle Eastern , American , and European partners to envision a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ underpinnings of the idea remain firm . The EU is India 's largest trading partner with bilateral trade in FY 2023-24 at $137.41 billion , and non-oil trade between India , the UAE and Saudi Arabia has increased significantly in recent years . The IMEC itself was meant to be more than a trade corridor . Its implementing partners would lay cables for " electricity and digital connectivity " , pipes for " clean hydrogen export " , to " increase efficiencies , reduce costs , enhance economic unity , generate jobs , and lower greenhouse gas emissions . " <p> From the perspective of trade facilitation and accessibility , the IMEC was meant to address several issues that continue to persist till date , including no corridor-wide tariff standardisation and low financial integration among corridor partners , lack of corridor-wide insurance , and widely differing port capacities . The ambitious cross-Saudi/UAE railway meant to transit goods between the corridor 's sea-legs was also significantly under-developed . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> However , these presented benign modality and sustainability challenges which could be mitigated through commitment and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , participants explicitly agreed to meet within sixty days " to develop and commit to an action plan with relevant timetables . " <p> Less than a month later , the Middle East plunged into an unprecedented conflict that continues till date , and the intended stakeholder meeting never occurred . <p> Gaza poses fundamental challenges <p> The underlying economic logic of the IMEC remains . However , its challenges have evolved from reconcilable to fundamental . The single most important issue is Israel 's increasingly unpopular war on Gaza , which has killed at least 61,000 people thus far . <p> The IMEC 's cornerstone is the ' Middle East-Europe ' connection , between Jordan and Israel . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Unlike in 2023 , Jordan-Israel relations are presently at a significant low , and are worsening due to the Israeli-American push for Jordan to absorb more of the Palestinian population . <p> Similarly , the potential for Saudi-Israel normalisation is much lower today than in 2023 . Riyadh has doubled down on the need for Israeli concessions towards Palestine while Israel 's appetite to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ In fact , Israel is presently focused on formally re-occupying and potentially re-settling the Gaza Strip , despite intensifying global opposition . <p> The direct downstream impact of Israel 's seemingly endless war is the worsening of even those challenges which could be mitigated through reconciled trade practices between stakeholders . <p> For instance , while the Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping ( which carries the bulk of Europe 's trade ) vindicated the need for the IMEC as a more secure alternative , the expansion of Israel 's war ( into Lebanon , Yemen , Syria , Iraq , and with Iran ) bodes high insurance premiums for any trade transiting the region . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> That said , the corridor remains vital for Israel even as it continues to hinder its implementation . For Israel , the IMEC represents the pinnacle of its economic integration into a region where it has historically fought for acceptance and recognition . <p> In September , 2024 , Benjamin Netanyahu held up a map at the UN showing states on the IMEC route as " blessed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " -- reflecting the IMEC 's role as an invaluable adhesive to bind Israel with the Arab world , minus Palestine . <h> Future of IMEC up in the air <p> While the western leg of the corridor is unlikely to materialise in the near future , the IMEC 's eastern leg benefits from the strategic partnerships that India has forged with the Arab states . <p> While India 's economic and strategic relationship with the UAE has the most depth , India is Saudi Arabia 's second largest trading partner and both states have had a strategic partnership since 2010 . These partnerships have yielded several instruments to bolster connectivity . For instance , Riyadh and Abu Dhabi both also allow the use of UPI for fund transfers and remittance payments , improving the potential for digital connectivity along the IMEC route . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Consequently , for India , progress on the IMEC corridor is very much possible . This is despite internecine issues between Arab states over trade modalities . The Saudi need to undercut the Emirati economic dominance of the region @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ imposed new tariffs specifically on those GCC states that have " free zones " offering preferential tax and customs treatments . Objectively , this is standard economic competition between two Gulf powerhouses competing for influence and investments . But for a broader corridor that requires a common vision , this is a strong hindrance . <p> In the long term , for the IMEC to be realised in its originally envisioned form , a secure and stable Middle East is an imperative . This implies that if the IMEC was seen as the fruit of the region 's unprecedented stability in 2023 , the regional architecture that brought about this stability will have to be recreated . <p> Since that architecture failed to endure , it is now evident that as long as principal issues such as that of Palestinian statehood are not addressed , any regional connectivity plan will inevitably be susceptible to renewed conflict . Global recognition of the unsustainability of Israel 's war is now apparent with more Western states both recognising the Palestinian state as well as reconsidering the terms of their support to Israel . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ use in Gaza , in response to Israel considering a broader re-occupation of the Strip , is a case in point . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> Given both its scale and scope , the IMEC is essentially now a ' day-after ' plan -- waiting for the resolution of the Middle East 's oldest conflict . Until then , efforts like the August meeting in New Delhi can only focus on modalities and trade facilitation , with implementation being contingent on conflict resolution . <p> Bashir Ali Abbas is a Senior Research Associate at the Council for Strategic and Defense Research , New Delhi

Will they be automatically released from prison ? <p> Titled ' Maximum period for which an under trial prisoner can be detained ' , section 436-A Code of Criminal Procedure ( CrPC ) , 1973. states that an undertrial prisoner can not be held in prison for a period exceeding the maximum period of punishment for his offence . Release in such a circumstance is a statutory obligation , and thus automatic . The section also states that a person who has spent at least half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for his particular offence may be released , provided the offence does not carry the penalty of death . In this situation , however , the release of the undertrial is not automatic but subject to the court 's discretion after it hears the public prosecutor . <p> Section 436-A was inserted in the CrPC in 2006 , due to concerns that many undertrials were being detained @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> PRELIMS ANSWER KEY <p> 1 . @@128006802 <p> This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you . Subscribe to enjoy similar stories . <p> The pictures are heartbreaking : convoys of United Nations-marked trucks inching toward bomb-scarred cities , desperate children clamoring for supplies . These images seem to prove that the international system is , at the very least , trying to help . Yet in every conflict I have studied -- Somalia , Afghanistan , Iraq , Syria , Yemen , Sudan , Ethiopia and Gaza -- the same trucks double as cash machines for warlords , militias and authoritarian regimes . <p> Aid diversion is a widespread problem in humanitarian operations . Unless the U.S. and other donors rewrite the rules so that aid ca n't be separated from accountability , they will keep subsidizing the conflicts they abhor . <p> Somalia shows how thoroughly diversion can be built into routine . Three clan cartels win most World Food Program transport contracts , skim 30% to 50% of the cargo , and then split the spoils with those who transport the food and those who control the displacement camps . Based on U.N @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in our study that barely one-eighth of donated food reaches intended households . <p> In Syria , former President Bashar al-Assad insisted that all aid be converted at a government-set rate to roughly half the market price , enabling the regime to pocket at least $60 ? million in 2020 alone , while blocking aid from reaching the opposition by designating it as " unsafe . " <p> In Ethiopia , U.S. Agency for International Development workers discovered that their implementing partner , the U.N . ' s World Food Program , was aware of industrial-scale theft by the Ethiopian military but failed to stop it . Large quantities of wheat were diverted to private mills to make flour for the army . <p> Gaza presents the longest-running case of diverted aid . The U.N . Relief and Works Agency , with a $2.48 ? billion annual budget in 2024 and 13,000 local staff , effectively provides most public services in Gaza . <p> That frees Hamas to use its resources for tunnels and rockets . In regions under its control , it taxes incoming aid and places loyalists on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ personnel joined the Oct. ? 7 , 2023 , attack lasted only months ; services resumed with no vetting reforms because , donors said , " there is no alternative . " <p> Diversion persists for several reasons . <p> First , the moral considerations are difficult : When officials weigh " people will die tomorrow " against " fighters will grow stronger next month , " tomorrow always wins . <p> Second , people give priority to institutional survival : The humanitarian sector employs some 570,000 people and until 2025 spent about $35 ? billion a year , and agencies that refuse armed groups ' terms lose access , budgets and jobs . <p> Third , adversaries are able to adapt : Warlords remain in place while aid workers rotate ; they open businesses posing as nongovernmental organizations and bill the U.N . for delivering cargo . <p> Add fear of donor backlash and the result is a continuing lack of accountability . Those who break the rules hold more leverage than those sworn to enforce them . <p> But accountability is still within reach if donors step up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cut funds because they find the scale of diversions unacceptable , even hard-line actors bend . When Washington paused food aid to Ethiopia in 2023 , diversion plunged , and the government grudgingly accepted QR-coded tracking . <p> The U.S. , the European Union and Gulf states combined supply more than 70% of global humanitarian budgets . Together , they could enforce five conditions on every grantee : <p> * Require nondiversion benchmarks . All access fees , escorts and local taxes must be disclosed in advance ; one missed benchmark triggers a 12-month funding pause . <p> * Build in insurance for whistle-blowers . Two percent of every grant pays for external audits and the legal defense of whistle-blowers . <p> * Create sunset clauses . Missions longer than 10 years shut down unless donors unanimously extend them after a public review . <p> * Fund innovation . Create dedicated funding streams for fintech tracking , QR-coded commodities and other tools that make diversion more difficult . <p> None of this requires rewriting international law . It 's simply about enabling donors to use the one lever they control @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , fuels migration pressure on Europe , and forces Gulf monarchies to spend twice -- first on aid , then on arms . Conditional funding flips those incentives . <p> Regimes that want to look legitimate on the global stage must choose : guns or food , not both . Boosting accountability would also blunt the common critique that Washington preaches good governance while financing bad actors through humanitarian back doors . <p> Critics say pausing aid is immoral , as civilians would starve . This risk is real but not as definite as how it is often presented . Typically , there is n't enough data to infer the effect that a pause will have . The June 2023 Ethiopia pause triggered dire warnings of widespread famine . While some people no doubt suffered , the warnings did n't materialize . Acute food insecurity and child malnutrition went down in 2023 compared with 2022 . <p> In Yemen , food-security analyses during the suspension were limited to southern Yemen , where the pause in aid did n't occur . Acute food insecurity did rise in these areas , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were at work : currency collapse , wage arrears , siege tactics . <p> Against the immediate risk of human suffering , donors must consider that allowing aid diversion could extend that risk for years . A cross-country analysis of 621 leaders in 123 countries from 1960 to 1999 showed that large , unconditional aid inflows help autocrats survive . World Bank data show that unconditional aid correlates with higher corruption and weaker rule of law . <p> Climate shocks , urban sieges and pricier grain will likely push humanitarian budgets beyond $50 ? billion within a decade . Without reform , much of that money will feed armies before children . Worse , each scandal makes future interventions politically toxic , putting civilians in real need at risk of not receiving help . The choice is stark : tighten the taps now or watch the well run dry . <p> Ms. Barak-Corren is a law professor and the Haim H. Cohn Chair in Human Rights at Hebrew University of Jerusalem .

@@128022493 <h> Tears of Gaza and the Memory of Fire <h> Share : <p> Vibeke L ? kkeberg'sTears of Gaza is not a conventional war documentary . It does not seek military balance , does not offer strategic context , and does not pretend to be neutral . What it does offer is unfiltered grief . Shot during and in the aftermath of Israel 's Operation Cast Lead ( 2008 -- 2009 ) , the film compiles harrowing footage captured by Palestinian cameramen on the ground , later woven together in Norway by L ? kkeberg . The result is not a political statement in the traditional sense , but a searing indictment of the global conscience . <p> The documentary does not feature experts or analysts . It features children . Children who watched their siblings burn . Children who dug through rubble for their parents ' bodies . Children who narrate not the theories of war but the texture of it -- what it smells like , what it sounds like , and what it means when silence falls too suddenly . <p> The documentary is a collection of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lingers . It does not look away when bodies are pulled from debris or when a child stares into the lens , searching for a reason no one can provide . These are not anonymous victims . They are named , crying , bleeding , and still very much alive . Their stories are not neatly resolved by the end credits . Most of them are not resolved at all . <p> What makes Tears of Gaza especially unsettling is that it is neither voyeuristic nor exploitative . It is confrontational . The footage is difficult to watch because the reality is unbearable , not because of how it is presented . The use of white phosphorus , the targeting of hospitals , UN schools , and ambulances , the starvation , the severing of limbs and lives -- these are not editorial claims but recorded evidence . There is no space for denial . <p> The film also indirectly raises questions about the global media 's selective visibility . Much of this footage never aired on Western networks . Many of these voices were never amplified in diplomatic chambers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ historical document of omission . " But what balance is possible between an F-16 and a child ? Between a tank and a father carrying his daughter 's remains in a plastic bag ? Tears of Gaza does not pretend that all suffering is equal .
